subtopics.name: Main thread, Looper, and Handler fundamentals
Use cases and when to introduce them
Missing, unknown, nullable, and default JSON fields
Local vs remote sources of truth
What to share vs keep platform-specific

questions.text: Why should an Android app not rely on regular in-memory singletons to preserve user progress after the app is backgrounded?

answers.text: Because Android reinitializes singleton objects whenever an Activity is recreated after a configuration change.
Because the app process can be killed while backgrounded, clearing ordinary process memory.
Because the garbage collector reclaims singletons once the last Activity referencing them is destroyed.
Because onTrimMemory() clears static caches on the app's behalf when the system is under memory pressure.

questions.explanation: In-memory objects live only inside the current app process, and Android can kill a backgrounded process at any time to reclaim resources. A singleton is not reclaimed by the garbage collector while the process lives, and onTrimMemory() is only a callback the app may implement, not automatic cleanup. Progress that must survive process death belongs in saved state or persistent storage.

questions.text: Which Android component is designed to expose a structured interface for sharing app-managed data with other apps?

answers.text: Activity
Service
ContentProvider
BroadcastReceiver

questions.explanation: A ContentProvider presents data through a standard provider interface. Activities own UI, services perform background work, and broadcast receivers react to broadcast events.

questions.text: A long-lived repository needs a Context only to access application resources. Which Context is safest to retain?

answers.text: The current Activity context, because it resolves themed resources for the visible screen.
The application context, because it is not tied to a specific Activity instance.
A View's context, because a View releases its context reference once it is detached.
A ContextWrapper around the Activity, because wrapping removes the underlying Activity reference.

questions.explanation: A long-lived object that retains an Activity context can keep that Activity and its view hierarchy reachable after it should be collected. An Activity context does resolve themed resources, and a View's context is normally the Activity itself, so neither is safe to retain. Wrapping an Activity in a ContextWrapper still delegates to it. The application context is scoped to the process and is appropriate for app-wide resource access.

questions.text: What is the main difference between an explicit Intent and an implicit Intent?

answers.text: An explicit Intent names a target component; an implicit Intent describes an action to resolve.
An explicit Intent is delivered directly; an implicit Intent matches only filters declared in the same app.
An explicit Intent can target another app's component; an implicit Intent stays inside the calling app.
An explicit Intent is resolved at compile time; an implicit Intent is resolved by the PackageManager.

questions.explanation: An explicit Intent names its target component directly. An implicit Intent describes an action and data, and the system resolves it at runtime against intent filters, including filters declared by other apps. Explicit Intents can also address components in other apps when those components are exported.

questions.text: Why should expensive disk or network work not run directly on Android's main thread?

answers.text: Because the main thread is allocated a smaller stack than background threads.
Because suspend functions must resume on a dispatcher other than Dispatchers.Main.
Because blocking the main thread prevents timely UI rendering and input processing.
Because StrictMode blocks disk and network access on the main thread in release builds.

questions.explanation: The main thread dispatches rendering and input. Blocking it with expensive work causes dropped frames and can trigger an ANR. Suspend functions may legitimately resume on Dispatchers.Main, and StrictMode is an opt-in development aid that reports violations rather than a release-time guard.

questions.text: What is the purpose of Android resource qualifiers such as layout-land or values-night?

answers.text: They mark resources as overridable by library modules during resource merging.
They generate a separate R class so each configuration has its own resource IDs.
They prevent Activity recreation when the matching configuration changes.
They provide alternative resources that Android selects for the current configuration.

questions.explanation: Qualifiers such as layout-land or values-night mark alternative resource directories that Android selects for the current device configuration. Resource IDs stay stable across configurations, so no per-configuration R class is generated, and qualifiers do not affect whether an Activity is recreated; that is controlled by android:configChanges.

questions.text: Why is onPause() a poor place to perform a long database write or network request?

answers.text: Because onPause() runs only after the next Activity has already become visible.
Because onPause() should return quickly, and long work can delay the next screen's transition.
Because lifecycle callbacks are dispatched on a background thread unless configured otherwise.
Because work started in onPause() is cancelled as soon as onStop() runs.

questions.explanation: onPause() runs before the next Activity resumes and is expected to return quickly, so long work there delays the transition and risks not finishing. Lifecycle callbacks are delivered on the main thread, and work started in onPause() is not automatically cancelled later; durable work belongs in a persistence or background-work mechanism.

questions.text: In a Fragment that uses Views, why should view references normally be cleared in onDestroyView() rather than onDestroy()?

answers.text: Because the Fragment's View lifecycle can end before the Fragment instance is destroyed.
Because onDestroy() runs before the Fragment's view hierarchy is detached.
Because the FragmentManager clears view references when the Fragment is detached.
Because onDestroyView() is skipped when the Fragment goes onto the back stack.

questions.explanation: A Fragment instance can outlive its view hierarchy, most visibly when the Fragment is placed on the back stack: the view is destroyed while the Fragment instance is retained. onDestroyView() runs in that case, and nothing clears view references automatically, so holding them past onDestroyView() retains obsolete Views and their Activity context.

questions.text: What usually happens to an Activity during an unhandled configuration change such as rotation?

answers.text: The same instance continues and receives onConfigurationChanged().
The Activity restarts without onDestroy() being called.
The Activity is destroyed and a new instance is created.
The process restarts so new resources can be loaded.

questions.explanation: By default Android destroys and recreates the Activity so it can load configuration-specific resources. The instance is only kept and given onConfigurationChanged() when the configuration is declared in android:configChanges. The process itself is not restarted, and the full destroy callbacks do run.

questions.text: Why can a ViewModel preserve UI state across rotation but not by itself guarantee recovery after system-initiated process death?

answers.text: Because a ViewModel is retained by the Activity instance, which is recreated on rotation.
Because the ViewModelStore is written to disk for rotation but not for process death.
Because process death preserves Activity fields while discarding ViewModel instances.
Because ViewModels are in-memory objects and process death clears that memory.

questions.explanation: A ViewModel is held in a ViewModelStore that survives configuration change, but it is an ordinary in-memory object: nothing is written to disk, and process death clears the whole process, including Activity fields. State that must survive process death needs SavedStateHandle, rememberSaveable, or persistent storage.

questions.text: Which kind of state is a good candidate for saved-state APIs such as rememberSaveable or SavedStateHandle?

answers.text: Small transient UI state needed to restore the screen after recreation.
Large cached API responses that must remain queryable while offline.
Open socket connections that should survive process death.
Authentication tokens that must persist across an app reinstall.

questions.explanation: Saved-state APIs restore small amounts of transient UI state after recreation, and the saved state bundle is size-limited. Large cached responses, live connections, and credentials that must outlive the install belong in a database, be re-established on demand, or use dedicated secure storage.

questions.text: What does a navigation back stack primarily represent?

answers.text: A registry of the destinations the app declared in its navigation graph.
An ordered history of entries determining the current and previous destinations.
The task stack the system maintains for the app's activities.
A saved-state bundle that is rewritten each time the user navigates forward.

questions.explanation: A back stack is the ordered history of visited entries, so the top entry is the current destination and the one beneath it is where Back returns. The set of declared destinations is the navigation graph, and the system task stack for activities is a separate Android concept.

questions.text: In a typical single-stack navigation flow, what should happen when the user presses Back from a detail destination that was pushed from a list destination?

answers.text: Navigate to the list destination again, creating a new entry for it.
Pop the entire back stack and return to the start destination.
Pop the detail entry so the previous list entry becomes current again.
Clear the detail entry's saved state but leave it on the back stack.

questions.explanation: Back pops the current top entry so the existing list entry becomes current again, preserving its state. Navigating forward to the list instead adds a duplicate entry and loses the original, which is a common back-stack bug.

questions.text: In the classic Android View system, what is the role of a ViewGroup?

answers.text: It manages the Activity's window and attaches the content view.
It contains child Views and participates in measuring and laying them out.
It owns the View lifecycle and dispatches lifecycle callbacks to its children.
It defines measurement rules that each child View must implement itself.

questions.explanation: A ViewGroup is a View that holds child Views and is responsible for measuring and positioning them according to its own layout rules. The window and content view are managed by the Activity, and each child measures itself in response to the constraints its parent passes down.

questions.text: What is the high-level order of work in the classic Android View rendering pipeline?

answers.text: Measure, layout, then draw.
Draw, layout, then measure.
Inflate, measure, then invalidate.
Layout, measure, then draw.

questions.explanation: The View system runs a measure pass to determine sizes, then a layout pass to assign positions, then a draw pass. Sizes must be known before positions can be assigned, so measure always precedes layout, and inflation happens earlier when the hierarchy is created rather than as part of each traversal.

questions.text: Why does RecyclerView rely on ViewHolder reuse for large lists?

answers.text: To keep a stable adapter position for each item across dataset changes.
To let DiffUtil compute item changes without using a background thread.
To reset each item's view state automatically when it is rebound.
To reduce repeated View inflation and allocation while scrolling.

questions.explanation: Reuse avoids inflating and allocating a new view hierarchy for every item that scrolls into view. Because a ViewHolder is recycled rather than recreated, its views keep whatever state the previous item left behind, so onBindViewHolder must set every mutable property explicitly. Adapter positions are not stable across dataset changes, which is why stable IDs and DiffUtil exist.

questions.text: Why should Compose UI be driven by observable state rather than directly mutating emitted UI nodes?

answers.text: Because Compose emits an immutable view tree that cannot be modified after creation.
Because composables describe UI from state and re-run when observed state changes.
Because composables run on a background thread where direct mutation is unsafe.
Because Compose reuses node instances, so mutations would leak between recompositions.

questions.explanation: Compose is declarative: a composable describes what the UI should look like for the current state, and Compose calls it again when observed state changes. The emitted nodes are managed by Compose rather than being a tree the caller mutates, so the way to change UI is to change the state it reads.

questions.text: What can cause a composable that reads Compose state to recompose?

answers.text: Any change to a plain var field captured by the composable.
An explicit call to invalidate() on the enclosing ComposeView.
A change to observable state read by that composable.
Any change to state read by a sibling composable in the same layout.

questions.explanation: Compose tracks reads of observable state such as MutableState. When that state changes, only the scopes that read it are invalidated and re-run. A plain var is not observable, so writing to it does not schedule recomposition, and state read by a sibling invalidates that sibling rather than this composable.

questions.text: What is the usual goal of state hoisting in Compose?

answers.text: Move state to an appropriate owner and pass current value plus events down.
Move state into a ViewModel so that no composable holds local state.
Reduce recomposition by removing state reads from the composable tree.
Let a child own the state and expose it upward through a callback.

questions.explanation: Hoisting moves state to an appropriate owner, often the lowest common ancestor that reads and writes it, and passes the current value down with events going up. That makes a composable stateless and reusable. Hoisting is not the same as pushing all state into a ViewModel: local state that no other composable needs can stay where it is.

questions.text: Which statements about Compose side-effect APIs are correct? Select all that apply.

answers.text: LaunchedEffect launches a coroutine scoped to the composition for its key set.
SideEffect runs its block before the composition has been applied.
DisposableEffect can clean up resources when the effect leaves composition or keys change.
rememberCoroutineScope launches its coroutine when the composable first enters composition.

questions.explanation: LaunchedEffect launches a coroutine tied to composition that restarts when its keys change, and DisposableEffect provides cleanup when its keys change or it leaves composition. SideEffect publishes state after a successful composition rather than before it, and rememberCoroutineScope only returns a scope; the caller decides when to launch, typically from an event handler.

questions.text: Why are stable item keys important in Compose lazy lists when items can be inserted, removed, or reordered?

answers.text: They let the list skip composing items that are outside the viewport.
They allow the list to reuse one composable instance for all items.
They let the list compute item heights before composition runs.
They preserve item identity across insertions, removals, and moves.

questions.explanation: Keys tell Compose which item is which across dataset changes, so remembered state and animations follow the item when it moves rather than staying with a position. Skipping off-screen items is what makes a lazy list lazy and happens regardless of keys.

questions.text: How can unstable parameter types affect Compose performance?

answers.text: They force every parameter to be wrapped in remember at the call site.
They can prevent Compose from skipping recomposition when inputs are unchanged.
They make Compose recompose the whole tree instead of the affected subtree.
They prevent the compiler from generating a restartable group for the composable.

questions.explanation: If Compose cannot prove a parameter's value is unchanged, it cannot skip the composable and re-runs it even when the inputs are effectively equal. That affects skippability of the individual composable rather than forcing a whole-tree recomposition, and stable or immutable models restore skipping.

questions.text: What is the purpose of semantics information in Compose?

answers.text: To describe how a composable should be measured and laid out.
To cache the composable's rendered output for use by screen readers.
To expose UI meaning and actions to accessibility services and testing APIs.
To register the composable with the Android View accessibility framework directly.

questions.explanation: The semantics tree is a parallel description of what the UI means and what it can do. Accessibility services and Compose testing APIs both read it, which is why tests query semantics rather than layout internals. Measurement and layout are described separately by modifiers, not by semantics.

questions.text: What does Kotlin's type system express when a variable has nullable type String? instead of non-null type String?

answers.text: Both types accept null at runtime, because the JVM erases nullability.
String is non-null, while String? is nullable.
String is nullable, while String? is non-null.
Nullability is enforced by the IDE inspector rather than by the compiler.

questions.explanation: String is a non-null type and String? is its nullable counterpart. The distinction is enforced by the compiler, which rejects assigning null to a non-null type and requires a null check before use of a nullable one. Kotlin also inserts runtime intrinsic checks, so nullability is more than an IDE hint, though values arriving from unannotated Java can still violate it.

questions.text: What does a Kotlin data class primarily generate from properties declared in its primary constructor?

answers.text: Structural equality plus a deep copy of every referenced property.
equals(), hashCode(), and toString() over all properties, including those in the body.
Value-oriented functions such as equals(), hashCode(), toString(), componentN(), and copy().
Immutable properties, so a data class cannot declare a var in its constructor.

questions.explanation: A data class generates equals(), hashCode(), toString(), componentN(), and copy() from the properties declared in its primary constructor. Properties declared in the class body are deliberately excluded from those members, and copy() is shallow: it copies references rather than cloning referenced objects.

questions.text: What is a Kotlin object declaration commonly used for?

answers.text: Declaring a single instance that is created lazily on first access.
Declaring a class whose instances are pooled and reused by the runtime.
Grouping extension functions so that they are resolved statically.
Declaring a value class that avoids allocation at runtime.

questions.explanation: An object declaration defines a singleton that is instantiated lazily the first time it is accessed. It is not a pooling mechanism, and avoiding allocation for a wrapper type is what value class does. Because the instance lives in process memory, any state it holds is lost when the process is killed.

questions.text: Why are sealed classes or sealed interfaces useful for modeling UI states or results?

answers.text: They permit new direct subclasses to be added by consumers of the library.
They give each subclass a generated equals() and copy() implementation.
They prevent a subclass from declaring any additional state or properties.
They model a closed set of known alternatives the compiler can enumerate.

questions.explanation: A sealed type restricts its direct subtypes to the same module, so the compiler knows the complete set and can verify that a when expression is exhaustive. That is what makes sealed hierarchies useful for UI state and result types. Generated equality and copy come from data classes, not from sealing.

questions.text: In Kotlin generics, what does declaration-site variance with out T indicate?

answers.text: The type parameter may appear in parameter positions but not in return types.
The type parameter is covariant, so it may be produced but not consumed.
The type parameter is checked at runtime instead of at compile time.
The type parameter must be a supertype of every argument passed in.

questions.explanation: Declaring out T makes T covariant, so Box<Dog> is usable where Box<Animal> is expected. Covariance is safe only in producing positions, which is why the compiler rejects out types in parameter positions. The mirror case, in T, is contravariant and allows consumption instead.

questions.text: Why can an inline function with a reified type parameter check T at runtime?

answers.text: Because the compiler passes a hidden Class token for every type parameter.
Because reified type parameters are retained in the class file's generic signature.
Because the inline function body is expanded at call sites with the concrete type.
Because the JVM keeps runtime type information for all generic parameters.

questions.explanation: Inlining substitutes the function body at each call site, so the compiler can replace T with the concrete type argument used there. That makes is checks and T::class possible. Ordinary generic parameters are erased, no hidden Class token is passed automatically, and generic signatures in the class file are metadata that does not make T usable in an is check.

questions.text: What is the difference between == and === in Kotlin?

answers.text: == checks structural equality; === checks referential equality.
== checks referential equality; === checks structural equality.
== compiles to a null-safe equals() call, and === is a synonym for it.
=== compares hashCode() values, while == compares field contents.

questions.explanation: == performs structural equality through a null-safe equals() call, while === tests whether two references point to the same instance. They are distinct operators: two equal data class instances compare true with == and false with ===. Equal hash codes never establish equality on their own.

questions.text: What is a practical risk of overusing Kotlin scope functions such as apply, also, let, run, and with?

answers.text: They capture the receiver strongly, extending its lifetime past the block.
They allocate a new lambda object per call, because they are not inlined.
They rebind `this` to the enclosing class inside a nested block.
They can obscure receiver or argument meaning when nested or mixed heavily.

questions.explanation: Scope functions differ in whether the subject is `this` or `it` and in what they return. Nesting or mixing them makes it ambiguous which receiver a given expression refers to, which hurts readability. They are inline functions, so they do not add per-call lambda allocation, and they do not extend the lifetime of the receiver.

questions.text: When can Kotlin sequences be useful compared with eager collection operations?

answers.text: When a short pipeline over a small list must avoid allocation overhead.
When a multi-step pipeline benefits from laziness and fewer intermediate lists.
When the pipeline must run concurrently across several threads.
When the result must be iterated repeatedly without recomputing the pipeline.

questions.explanation: A sequence evaluates lazily and element by element, so a long chain of operations avoids materializing a list at every step. For a short chain over a small collection the eager version is usually faster, since sequences add per-element indirection. Sequences are also single-pass by nature and do not introduce concurrency.

questions.text: Why does JVM type erasure matter when designing generic Kotlin APIs for Android?

answers.text: Because erasure applies to Kotlin generics but not to Java generics on the JVM.
Because erasure drops variance annotations, so `out` has no compile-time effect.
Because generic type arguments are generally not directly available at runtime.
Because erasure loads a separate copy of a generic class per type argument.

questions.explanation: Both Kotlin and Java generics are erased on the JVM, so a generic type argument is generally not recoverable at runtime. APIs that need the actual type must take an explicit Class or KClass token or use an inline function with a reified parameter. Variance is a compile-time checking rule, and a generic class is loaded once regardless of how many type arguments are used.

questions.text: What does a suspend function indicate in Kotlin?

answers.text: It runs on a dedicated thread pool separate from the calling thread.
It can suspend without blocking the thread and resume later.
It resumes execution on the same thread where it was suspended.
It can be called from an ordinary function without a coroutine context.

questions.explanation: A suspend function can pause without holding the underlying thread, freeing that thread for other work until the function resumes. It does not imply a particular thread or pool: the dispatcher decides where it runs, and it may resume on a different thread. It also cannot be called from ordinary code, only from another suspend function or a coroutine builder.

questions.text: When is async more appropriate than launch?

answers.text: When the coroutine must survive cancellation of its parent scope.
When the work should start eagerly before the scope becomes active.
When the caller needs a result value that can be awaited later.
When the coroutine must run on a dispatcher different from the caller.

questions.explanation: async returns a Deferred whose value is retrieved with await, which is what makes it the right choice when the caller needs a result. launch returns a Job for fire-and-forget work. Neither builder changes cancellation semantics or the dispatcher on its own; withContext changes the dispatcher and a different scope or NonCancellable governs cancellation.

questions.text: What problem does structured concurrency address?

answers.text: It ties coroutine lifetimes to explicit scopes and parent-child relationships.
It makes every child coroutine share the dispatcher of its parent scope.
It serializes child coroutines so that only one runs at a time.
It restarts a failed child coroutine inside the same parent scope.

questions.explanation: Structured concurrency gives every coroutine a parent, so a scope does not complete until its children do, cancellation propagates down, and failures propagate up. It is about lifetime and ownership rather than scheduling: children inherit context but can override the dispatcher, and they still run concurrently.

questions.text: Why should long-running coroutine loops check for cancellation or call cancellable suspending functions?

answers.text: Because cancellation interrupts the underlying thread the coroutine runs on.
Because a cancelled coroutine finishes its current block before stopping.
Because cancellation takes effect only at the next dispatcher switch.
Because cancellation is cooperative and busy code only stops at a check.

questions.explanation: Cancellation sets the Job to cancelling and relies on the coroutine to notice. Suspending functions in kotlinx.coroutines check for it, but a tight CPU-bound loop that never suspends keeps running. Such code should call ensureActive(), yield(), or test isActive. Cancellation does not interrupt the thread.

questions.text: How does a regular Job parent usually react when one child coroutine fails with an uncaught exception?

answers.text: It keeps its other children running and reports the failure to a handler.
It is cancelled, and sibling children are cancelled as a consequence.
It waits for the remaining children to finish before propagating.
It suspends until a CoroutineExceptionHandler decides whether to cancel.

questions.explanation: With a regular Job, a child failure cancels the parent, which cancels the remaining children and propagates the exception. Isolating siblings so that one failure does not cancel the others is exactly what SupervisorJob or supervisorScope provides, and a CoroutineExceptionHandler only handles an exception that has already propagated to the root.

questions.text: What is withContext commonly used for in Android coroutine code?

answers.text: Starting a child coroutine that runs concurrently with the caller.
Running a block on another dispatcher without waiting for its result.
Switching execution context for a scoped block of suspending work.
Replacing the dispatcher for every coroutine in the current scope.

questions.explanation: withContext runs a block with a modified context, most often moving blocking IO onto Dispatchers.IO, and it suspends until that block returns its result. It does not start concurrent work, which is what launch and async do, and its effect is scoped to the block rather than to the surrounding scope.

questions.text: What makes a basic Kotlin Flow cold?

answers.text: Its producer block runs only when a collector starts collecting.
It replays the most recent value to each new collector.
It shares a single active producer among all of its collectors.
It continues emitting after its last collector stops.

questions.explanation: A cold flow is inert until collected, and each collection runs the producer again from the start, so two collectors get two independent executions. Holding a latest value, sharing a single producer, and emitting without collectors are all properties of hot flows such as StateFlow and SharedFlow.

questions.text: What does flowOn affect in a Kotlin Flow pipeline?

answers.text: The terminal collector and any operators applied after it.
The whole pipeline, including the collector's own context.
The dispatcher used by the coroutine that calls collect.
The upstream part of the flow before the flowOn operator.

questions.explanation: flowOn changes the context for operators upstream of it, which is how emission is moved off the collector's thread. Everything downstream, including collect, keeps the collector's context. That preservation is what makes flows context-transparent, and it is why flowOn is placed after the operators it should affect.

questions.text: When is StateFlow a good fit for exposing UI state from a ViewModel?

answers.text: When each collector must receive its own one-time navigation event.
When the UI needs the latest state value and updates when it changes.
When every intermediate value must be delivered without conflation.
When the stream must start without an initial value.

questions.explanation: StateFlow always holds a current value, requires an initial value, and emits the latest state to each collector, which matches screen state that the UI re-renders from. It conflates fast updates, so intermediate values can be skipped, and it replays the current value to every collector, which makes it a poor fit for one-time events; SharedFlow or a Channel suits those better.

questions.text: Which statements about SharedFlow are correct? Select all that apply.

answers.text: It is a hot flow that emits independently of collectors.
It exposes a current value that new collectors read immediately.
It completes once all of its collectors have cancelled.
Its replay cache size is configurable at construction.

questions.explanation: SharedFlow is hot: it exists and can emit whether or not anyone is collecting, and it broadcasts each emission to all active collectors. Its replay cache is configurable, from zero for pure events upward. Always exposing a current value is the defining property of StateFlow, and a SharedFlow does not complete when collectors go away.

questions.text: Why is separation of concerns important in Android architecture?

answers.text: It ensures each feature is built from exactly one layer of abstraction.
It removes the need for integration tests between the layers.
It keeps responsibilities focused so changes and tests touch smaller parts.
It requires each layer to depend on the layer directly above it.

questions.explanation: Giving UI, state holding, data access, and business rules distinct responsibilities narrows the blast radius of a change and lets each part be tested in isolation. It does not remove the need for tests across boundaries, and dependencies should point inward toward policy rather than upward toward the UI.

questions.text: In unidirectional data flow, how do state and events usually move?

answers.text: State flows down to consumers, and events flow up to the state owner.
State and events both travel downward from the owner to the UI.
Events travel down to the UI, and state is pushed back upward.
Each UI component owns its state and synchronises peers directly.

questions.explanation: State moves in one direction, from its owner down to the UI that renders it, while user interactions move back up as events the owner interprets. Keeping those directions separate is what makes the flow predictable: the UI never mutates state directly, and components do not synchronise with each other behind the owner's back.

questions.text: What role does a repository usually play in Android app architecture?

answers.text: It exposes database entities directly to the UI layer.
It coordinates access to one or more data sources behind a focused API.
It owns the lifecycle of the screens that consume its data.
It holds the UI state a screen renders after configuration change.

questions.explanation: A repository owns access to app data, deciding between local and remote sources and exposing results in domain terms. Keeping persistence types behind that boundary is part of its purpose. Screen state and lifecycle belong to the state holder, typically a ViewModel, not to the repository.

questions.text: What does single source of truth mean for a piece of application data?

answers.text: Each screen keeps its own copy and reconciles differences later.
The most recently updated source wins whenever two copies disagree.
Each layer caches the data so no layer depends on another.
One owner is responsible for the data and exposes it to consumers.

questions.explanation: One owner is authoritative for a piece of data and every consumer reads it from there, so there is nothing to reconcile. Per-screen copies or per-layer caches reintroduce exactly the conflicting-copy problem the pattern avoids, and a last-writer-wins rule is a conflict-resolution policy rather than a single source of truth.

questions.text: Why should UI state have a clear owner?

answers.text: So state changes have one responsible place and are exposed predictably.
So any child can mutate the shared backing field when it needs to.
So state survives process death without any saved-state handling.
So the UI layer can read state without observing it.

questions.explanation: A single owner decides how state changes and publishes it as observable, read-only state to consumers. That prevents conflicting updates from several places. Ownership is separate from durability: surviving process death still requires saved state or persistence regardless of who owns the value.

questions.text: What problem does dependency inversion help solve between domain logic and data implementations?

answers.text: It moves the interface into the data layer next to its implementation.
It removes the need for any dependency-injection container at runtime.
It keeps higher-level policy from depending on concrete implementations.
It replaces compile-time dependencies with reflection-based lookup.

questions.explanation: Dependency inversion has higher-level policy depend on an abstraction that the policy side owns, while the concrete implementation depends on that abstraction. Placing the interface next to its implementation in the data layer keeps the arrow pointing the wrong way and defeats the purpose. Inversion is about direction, not about removing runtime wiring.

questions.text: When is adding a use-case layer most defensible in an Android feature?

answers.text: Whenever a screen needs to read from more than one repository.
When it holds business rules or orchestration that would otherwise be duplicated.
When the ViewModel needs to call a suspending repository function.
When the team wants every repository call wrapped for the sake of consistency.

questions.explanation: A use case earns its place when it holds real logic: rules, orchestration across sources, or behaviour that several callers would otherwise duplicate. Reading from two repositories or calling a suspending function is something a ViewModel can do directly, and adding a pass-through layer purely for uniformity adds indirection without moving any logic.

questions.text: Why is constructor injection often preferred for required dependencies?

answers.text: It makes required dependencies explicit at construction time.
It defers dependency resolution until the dependency is first used.
It lets a class resolve its own dependencies from a container.
It allows optional dependencies to be omitted at construction.

questions.explanation: Taking required collaborators as constructor parameters makes them visible in the type, allows them to be held in immutable properties, and guarantees the object is fully formed once constructed. A test can then supply fakes by calling the constructor. Resolving dependencies internally from a container is the service-locator approach and hides the same information.

questions.text: What is the role of a composition root in manual dependency injection?

answers.text: It provides a global registry that classes query for their dependencies.
It defines the scopes and lifetimes that the DI framework enforces.
It centralizes construction and wiring of application dependencies.
It caches constructed objects so each type is created only once.

questions.explanation: The composition root is the single place near the application entry point where the object graph is assembled, so wiring decisions live in one reviewable location. A registry that classes query at runtime is a service locator, which reintroduces hidden dependencies, and caching or scoping is a separate concern from where construction happens.

questions.text: Which statements about DI scopes are correct? Select all that apply.

answers.text: A scope guarantees a new instance at each injection point.
A scope controls the lifetime and sharing boundary of provided instances.
A longer-lived component can safely hold a shorter-lived dependency.
Incorrect scoping can create leaks or unintended shared state.

questions.explanation: A scope defines how long a provided instance lives and which consumers share it, from per-request instances up to application singletons. Getting it wrong matters in both directions: too wide and short-lived objects such as an Activity are retained past their lifetime, too narrow and objects that should be shared are rebuilt. A long-lived holder retaining a short-lived dependency is the classic leak.

questions.text: What is a common downside of a service locator compared with explicit dependency injection?

answers.text: It resolves dependencies at compile time rather than at runtime.
It can hide dependencies and lifecycle assumptions behind runtime lookup.
It prevents the same instance from being shared between consumers.
It requires every dependency to be declared as a constructor parameter.

questions.explanation: With a service locator a class reaches into a registry to fetch collaborators, so its dependencies no longer appear in its signature. That makes them invisible to callers and tests, and a missing registration fails at runtime rather than at compile time. Declaring dependencies as constructor parameters is the alternative it is being contrasted with.

questions.text: Which storage option is usually appropriate for small key-value user preferences that must remain available across app restarts?

answers.text: SavedStateHandle, which restores screen state after recreation.
DataStore, which persists key-value or typed data to disk.
Room, which stores structured relational data with queries.
A file in the app's cacheDir, which the system may clear.

questions.explanation: DataStore is the Jetpack option for small preference or typed data that must outlive the process. SavedStateHandle only restores a screen after recreation and does not persist across restarts, cacheDir may be cleared by the system when storage is low, and Room is the right tool for larger structured data that needs queries rather than a handful of preferences.

questions.text: What is the responsibility of a Room DAO?

answers.text: Declaring the tables and columns that Room should create.
Configuring the database version and its migrations.
Declaring the queries and access methods for the database.
Mapping database rows into domain models for the UI.

questions.explanation: A DAO declares the queries and access methods Room generates implementations for. Tables and columns are described by @Entity classes, the version and migrations belong to the @Database class, and translating persistence rows into domain models is normally the repository's job so Room types stay behind the data layer.

questions.text: Why are database transactions important when multiple related writes must succeed or fail together?

answers.text: They make a group of related writes commit or roll back together.
They allow concurrent writers to modify the same rows safely.
They keep the database connection open so later queries run faster.
They defer writes until the app moves to the background.

questions.explanation: A transaction makes several statements atomic: either all of them are committed or none are, so a failure part way through cannot leave a half-updated database. That is a consistency guarantee rather than a performance or scheduling feature, and it does not make concurrent writes to the same rows safe on its own.

sources.title: Save Data in a Local Database Using Room

questions.text: What is useful about returning Flow from a Room query?

answers.text: It streams rows one at a time as the underlying cursor is read.
It keeps the query result synchronised with the remote server.
It runs the query on the main thread without blocking it.
It lets collectors receive updated query results as data changes.

questions.explanation: An observable Room query re-runs and re-emits whenever the tables it reads are modified, so the UI can observe local data and stay current without polling. Each emission is a complete query result rather than a stream of individual rows, and Room knows nothing about remote data.

sources.title: Save Data in a Local Database Using Room

questions.text: In an offline-first app, why is a local data source commonly treated as the source of truth?

answers.text: Because the local copy is newer than the server whenever the two differ.
Because the app stays usable and consistent when the network is unavailable.
Because reading from disk removes the need to handle network errors.
Because the server is treated as a cache in front of the local database.

questions.explanation: Reads are served from local storage, so the UI has data immediately and behaves the same whether or not the network is reachable, while synchronisation updates that local store in the background. The remote source is still authoritative for data the device did not create; the local database is the source the UI reads from, not a claim that local data is always fresher.

questions.text: Why does HTTP idempotency matter when designing retry behavior?

answers.text: It means the server returns an identical response body on every call.
It means the request can be retried without any backoff delay.
It indicates whether retrying a request may repeat unintended side effects.
It means the request is certain to succeed on a later attempt.

questions.explanation: An idempotent request produces the same server-side effect whether it is made once or several times, which is what makes automatic retry safe. It says nothing about the response body, which may legitimately differ between calls, and nothing about whether a retry will succeed or how it should be paced. Non-idempotent operations such as many POSTs need an idempotency key to be retried safely.

questions.text: Why should Android network clients configure timeouts?

answers.text: To limit the total number of retries for a failed call.
To bound waiting time for network operations that may stall.
To cap the size of a response body the client will buffer.
To stop idle pooled connections from being reused later.

questions.explanation: Connect, read, and write timeouts bound how long the client waits at each stage, so a stalled server or a half-open connection fails in bounded time instead of holding resources and leaving the user waiting. Retry counts, response size limits, and connection-pool behaviour are configured separately.

questions.text: What is a common use of an OkHttp interceptor?

answers.text: Adding headers and observing or modifying requests and responses.
Defining the endpoint paths and HTTP methods for a service.
Converting response bodies into Kotlin data classes.
Configuring the connection and read timeouts for the client.

questions.explanation: An interceptor sits in the call chain and can inspect, rewrite, short-circuit, or retry a request and its response, which suits cross-cutting concerns such as authentication headers and logging. Declaring endpoints is Retrofit's role, body conversion belongs to a converter factory, and timeouts are set on the OkHttpClient builder.

questions.text: What is the benefit of declaring Retrofit service functions as suspend functions?

answers.text: They retry the request automatically whenever the call fails.
They allow a service interface to be used without a base URL.
They remove the need for a converter factory on the client.
They integrate asynchronous calls with coroutine suspension.

questions.explanation: Declaring a service function as suspend lets Retrofit deliver the result through coroutine suspension, so the call fits structured concurrency: it can be cancelled with its scope and composed with other suspending work without callbacks. Body conversion, base URL configuration, and retry behaviour are unchanged and still configured on the client.

sources.title: Retrofit Changelog: Kotlin suspend Function Support

questions.text: What is a key difference between kotlinx.serialization and reflection-heavy JSON libraries?

answers.text: It resolves serializers by reflecting over properties at runtime.
It uses compiler-assisted serializers and supports Kotlin Multiplatform.
It serializes any class without requiring an annotation or plugin.
It requires each model to implement a serializer interface by hand.

questions.explanation: The kotlinx.serialization compiler plugin generates a serializer for each @Serializable class at compile time. Because nothing depends on runtime reflection, it works on Kotlin/Native and Kotlin/JS as well as the JVM, and missing serializers are reported when compiling rather than when the model is first parsed.

questions.text: A deferrable sync should survive process death and run only when network connectivity is available. Which API is the best fit?

answers.text: A background thread held by an application-scoped singleton.
A coroutine launched in the ViewModel's scope.
WorkManager with a required-network constraint.
A LaunchedEffect that starts when the screen appears.

questions.explanation: WorkManager persists its work queue, so enqueued work survives process death and reboot, and constraints let the system defer it until connectivity is available. Every other option is tied to something shorter-lived: a ViewModel scope ends with the screen, a LaunchedEffect ends when the composable leaves composition, and a thread in a singleton dies with the process.

questions.text: When is a foreground service generally appropriate?

answers.text: For user-noticeable ongoing work that must always show a notification.
For deferrable sync that should run when the device is charging.
For work that must finish after the user swipes the app away.
For periodic polling that should continue while the screen is off.

questions.explanation: A foreground service is for work the user is actively aware of and expects to continue, such as playback or navigation, and it must show an ongoing notification. Deferrable or periodic background work belongs to WorkManager, which the system can schedule under battery and connectivity constraints instead of keeping a service alive.

questions.text: For apps targeting modern Android versions, why do foreground service types matter?

answers.text: They select which notification channel the ongoing service posts to.
They declare the foreground work category and related requirements.
They exempt the service from background execution limits.
They set the priority the scheduler gives to the service.

questions.explanation: The declared type states what category of user-visible work the service performs, and recent Android versions require it along with the matching permissions and runtime prerequisites for that category. It is a declaration of purpose that the platform enforces, not an exemption from restrictions or a scheduling hint.

questions.text: Why should Android apps choose background APIs with OS limits in mind?

answers.text: Because background restrictions apply only to apps targeting older SDKs.
Because background work is billed against a per-app CPU quota the OS enforces.
Because background APIs behave identically across all manufacturers.
Because the OS restricts background execution to protect battery and system health.

questions.explanation: Android constrains what apps may do in the background through doze, app standby buckets, and background start restrictions, so work scheduled with the wrong API may be delayed indefinitely or refused. Choosing an API that expresses deferrability and constraints lets the system run the work at a time it will actually succeed. Manufacturers also add their own restrictions on top.

questions.text: Why do Android notification channels matter?

answers.text: They determine which activity opens when a notification is tapped.
They group related notifications into a single expandable summary.
They give users category-level control over notification behavior.
They set an importance the app can raise later without the user.

questions.explanation: Channels are the unit of user control: the user can mute, change importance, or alter behaviour per category rather than for the app as a whole. Once a channel is created the app cannot raise its importance again, only the user can. Bundling related notifications is done with groups, and the tap target comes from the PendingIntent.

questions.text: For Android 13 and higher, what must most apps do before posting non-exempt notifications?

answers.text: Declare POST_NOTIFICATIONS in the manifest, which grants it.
Request the POST_NOTIFICATIONS runtime permission from the user.
Create a notification channel, which implies the permission.
Raise the app's targetSdkVersion to re-enable notifications.

questions.explanation: From Android 13, POST_NOTIFICATIONS is a runtime permission: it must be declared in the manifest and then requested from the user, who can decline. Declaring it alone is not enough, and creating a channel does not grant it. Posting without the grant silently fails for non-exempt notifications.

questions.text: What is a practical difference between FCM notification messages and data messages?

answers.text: Data messages go to app code; the SDK can display notification messages.
Data messages are displayed by the system when the app is backgrounded.
Notification messages are delivered to onMessageReceived in every app state.
Data messages are given higher delivery priority than notification messages.

questions.explanation: A data message carries a key-value payload that is handed to the app to act on, so the app decides whether anything is shown. A notification message can be rendered by the SDK without app code when the app is in the background, and only reaches onMessageReceived while the app is in the foreground. Priority is set per message rather than implied by the type.

questions.text: Why should Android test strategy include more than only end-to-end UI tests?

answers.text: Because UI tests cannot assert on state held inside a ViewModel.
Because focused lower-level tests run faster and isolate failures precisely.
Because unit tests also catch integration problems between separate modules.
Because end-to-end tests can run only on physical devices.

questions.explanation: A test suite made only of end-to-end tests is slow and reports failures far from their cause, so a regression means bisecting a long path. Smaller tests around units and boundaries run in seconds and point at the responsible code. They do not replace integration coverage, which is why a mix is recommended rather than only one level.

questions.text: What is a common reason to use a fake implementation in a unit test?

answers.text: To record which methods were called and assert on that afterwards.
To run the real implementation with logging added around it.
To replace a dependency with deterministic behavior under test.
To skip the dependency entirely by returning null from it.

questions.explanation: A fake is a working implementation with simplified behaviour, such as an in-memory repository, so the class under test exercises a realistic contract deterministically. Recording calls and asserting on them describes a mock or spy, which verifies interactions instead of behaviour and couples the test to how the code is written.

questions.text: Why are ViewModels often good candidates for local unit tests?

answers.text: Their state transitions can often be tested without rendering UI.
They expose state as plain fields that tests can read synchronously.
They run on the main thread, so tests need no dispatcher control.
They hold no state between events, so each test starts from clean state.

questions.explanation: A ViewModel maps inputs to observable state without touching the view hierarchy, so with fake dependencies its transitions can be asserted in a fast local test. That still requires handling asynchrony: state is usually exposed as a Flow and coroutines need a test dispatcher, so reading a value synchronously is not generally possible.

questions.text: What is the purpose of runTest in coroutine tests?

answers.text: To run every test on a real background thread pool.
To catch exceptions thrown by child coroutines and ignore them.
To make delay() suspend for its real wall-clock duration in tests.
To test suspending code with a controlled coroutine test environment.

questions.explanation: runTest provides a scope backed by a test scheduler that skips delays using virtual time, so a coroutine that waits ten seconds completes immediately while ordering is preserved. It also waits for child coroutines and surfaces their failures rather than swallowing them.

questions.text: Why do Compose UI tests often query by semantics rather than implementation details?

answers.text: Because semantics are generated from the layout node hierarchy.
Because semantics expose meaningful UI information to tests and accessibility.
Because semantics let a test read a composable's remembered state.
Because Compose provides no stable identifier for a composable function.

questions.explanation: The semantics tree describes what the UI means and what can be done with it, and it is the same tree accessibility services consume. Querying it keeps tests aligned with observable behaviour, so refactoring layout structure does not break them. Semantics describe meaning rather than layout, and they do not expose internal remembered state.

questions.text: What is a common cause of an ANR in an Android app?

answers.text: Allocating many short-lived objects during scrolling.
Running a database query on Dispatchers.IO.
Blocking the main thread with long-running work.
Holding a wake lock while the screen is off.

questions.explanation: An ANR is raised when the main thread fails to handle input or a lifecycle event within the system's time limit, so the usual cause is long synchronous work such as disk or network access on that thread. Moving the work to another dispatcher is the fix, not the cause. Heavy allocation can cause jank through collection pauses without producing an ANR.

questions.text: How can retaining an Activity reference in a singleton cause a memory leak?

answers.text: The singleton can keep the Activity reachable after its lifecycle should end.
The Activity is copied into the singleton, doubling its memory use.
The garbage collector cannot reclaim objects that override finalize().
The singleton keeps a weak reference that the collector ignores.

questions.explanation: A singleton lives as long as the process, so a strong reference from it keeps the destroyed Activity and its entire view hierarchy reachable and therefore uncollectable. Nothing is copied; the leak is that one reference. A weak reference would be the fix, since the collector is free to reclaim through it.

questions.text: What is a reasonable way to reduce unnecessary recomposition work in Compose?

answers.text: Hoist every piece of state to the top-level composable.
Wrap each composable call in remember to cache its output.
Read state as high in the tree as possible so that reads are shared.
Use stable models and scope state changes to where they are needed.

questions.explanation: Compose skips a composable when it can prove its inputs are unchanged, so stable types plus state read close to where it is used keeps invalidation small. Reading state high in the tree has the opposite effect: everything below is invalidated together. remember caches a value across recomposition rather than caching emitted UI.

questions.text: Why should expensive initialization be treated carefully during app startup?

answers.text: Because work in Application.onCreate() runs on a background thread.
Because synchronous startup work can delay first draw and user interaction.
Because the system kills apps whose cold start exceeds a fixed budget.
Because content providers are initialized after the first frame is drawn.

questions.explanation: Application.onCreate() and content-provider initialization both run on the main thread before the first activity draws, so every synchronous library initialized there is added directly to cold-start time. Deferring non-critical work or initializing it lazily keeps the first frame early; the system does not enforce a hard startup budget.

questions.text: Why should an app request a runtime permission close to the user action that needs it?

answers.text: Because a permission requested at startup is denied without a prompt.
Because a later request is granted without showing a dialog.
Because contextual requests explain the purpose and improve user trust.
Because the system revokes permissions not requested in context.

questions.explanation: A request made at the moment the feature needs it carries its own justification, so the user can see why access is required and is more likely to grant it. A request at launch is still shown and can still be granted, but without context it is more often denied, and a denial is harder to recover from than never having asked.

questions.text: Why should exported Android components be reviewed carefully?

answers.text: Because other apps on the device may be able to invoke them.
Because exported components run in a separate process by default.
Because exporting makes a component visible only to signed apps.
Because exported components bypass the app's own permission checks.

questions.explanation: Exporting makes a component part of the app's external attack surface: any app on the device can send it an Intent, so its inputs are untrusted and must be validated, and access should be limited with permissions or by not exporting it. Exporting changes visibility only; it does not change the process the component runs in or disable permission checks.

questions.text: Why should access tokens, personal data, and secrets be excluded from logs?

answers.text: Because logcat output is attached to every crash report by default.
Because log entries are retained on the device indefinitely.
Because the system redacts tokens from logcat in release builds.
Because logs can expose sensitive data beyond its intended boundary.

questions.explanation: Log output is read during debugging, captured in bug reports, and shared with support, so anything written there escapes the boundary the data was collected under. Nothing redacts it automatically, which is why tokens, credentials, and personal data should never be logged rather than logged and relied on to be stripped later.

questions.text: Why does Gradle distinguish dependency configurations such as implementation, api, and runtimeOnly?

answers.text: To decide which repository each dependency is downloaded from.
To model how dependencies are declared, resolved, and exposed.
To control the order in which the modules are compiled.
To pin the version that transitive dependencies resolve to.

questions.explanation: A configuration expresses the role a dependency plays: implementation keeps it off the consumer's compile classpath, api exposes it to consumers, and runtimeOnly excludes it from compilation entirely. Choosing implementation over api is what keeps module rebuilds narrow. Repository selection and version resolution are configured separately.

questions.text: What problem do Gradle version catalogs solve in a multi-module project?

answers.text: They resolve version conflicts between transitive dependencies.
They cache dependency artifacts so that builds work offline.
They centralize dependency coordinates and versions behind aliases.
They enforce that every module uses the same dependency set.

questions.explanation: A version catalog declares dependency and plugin coordinates once and exposes them as type-safe aliases, so modules stop repeating literal versions and an upgrade is a single edit. It is a declaration mechanism: conflict resolution between transitive versions and artifact caching remain Gradle's normal resolution behaviour.

questions.text: What is a key difference between an APK and an Android App Bundle?

answers.text: An APK is installable; an App Bundle is a publishing format for generating APKs.
An App Bundle is installed directly and an APK is generated from it later.
An APK is unsigned, while an App Bundle carries the signing key.
An App Bundle is an APK compressed with a different algorithm.

questions.explanation: An APK is what a device installs. An App Bundle is uploaded to the store, which uses it to generate and sign APKs tailored to each device's density, ABI, and language, so users download less. A device cannot install a bundle directly.

questions.text: A news app must remain readable during poor connectivity. Which design choice best supports that requirement?

answers.text: Show a loading state until the newest articles have finished downloading.
Read from a local source of truth and sync remote updates in the background.
Keep responses in an in-memory cache for the current session.
Retry failed requests immediately until the network recovers.

questions.explanation: Rendering from a persistent local store means the article list is available immediately and stays readable with no connectivity, while background synchronisation refreshes it when possible. An in-memory cache disappears with the process, and blocking on the network or retrying tightly makes the poor-connectivity case worse rather than better.

questions.text: When designing background sync for mobile, which constraints should be considered? Select all that apply.

answers.text: Network availability and whether the connection is metered.
Battery level and whether the device is charging.
The exact wall-clock time at which each sync must run.
OS background execution limits and the retry policy.

questions.explanation: Background sync must respect connectivity and metering, battery and charging state, and the platform's background execution limits, with a backoff policy for failures. Exact wall-clock timing is not something background sync can rely on: the system batches and defers deferrable work, so a design that needs precise timing is using the wrong mechanism.

questions.text: What is a good rule of thumb when deciding what to put in Kotlin Multiplatform common code?

answers.text: Put all code in commonMain and add expect/actual wherever it fails to compile.
Share only data models and keep all behaviour in platform code.
Share platform-independent logic and use platform source sets for platform APIs.
Duplicate logic per platform so each target can diverge freely.

questions.explanation: Code belongs in common when the concept itself is platform-independent, such as domain rules, validation, and data transformation. Reaching for expect/actual whenever common code fails to compile inverts that test and produces a shared layer full of platform holes. Limited duplication is preferable to a shared abstraction that fits no platform well.

questions.text: What problem do expect and actual declarations solve in Kotlin Multiplatform?

answers.text: They let common code call a declaration that every platform implements itself.
They generate the platform implementations from the common declaration.
They let common code call platform APIs with no implementation needed.
They allow a common class to inherit from a platform-specific type.

questions.explanation: An expect declaration defines the contract common code compiles against, and every target must supply a matching actual, which the compiler checks. Nothing is generated automatically: the point is that the developer writes each platform implementation behind one shared signature. Where a plain interface plus constructor injection suffices, that is usually the simpler option.
